terms.grammar: adjective, third declension; with the genitive or the dative
evidence: Cic. Sen. 80: nihil esse mortī tam simile quam somnum
Ter. Ad. 411: est similis majōrum suum
terms.comment: What a thing is like goes in the genitive in Plautus and Terence (tuī similis, like you); Cicero keeps the genitive for persons and uses the dative for things, and after Augustus the dative is usual (Lewis & Short). Alike, of two or more, is inter sē similēs; the opposite is dissimilis (see different).

evidence: Cic. Pis. 93: statuam istīus persimilem (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: just like, similar in every way
terms.comment: Most frequent in Plautus, Terence and Lucretius (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: neque aqua aquae nec lacte est lactis, crēde mī, usquam similius, quam hic tuī est, tūque hujus autem
phrases.english: water is not more like water, nor milk more like milk, believe me, than he is like you and you like him

phrases.latin: jam vērō vidētis nihil esse mortī tam simile quam somnum
phrases.english: and you see that nothing is so like death as sleep

phrases.latin: incidī in māteriam vēram sed simillimam fictae
phrases.english: I have come upon a story that is true, but very like a made-up one
